Chapter One

The street had moved eleven yards since the previous evening, and Meera Roy was the only person in Calcutta who had drawn it well enough to notice.

At half past seven, the Survey Office in Hastings smelled of lampblack, camphor, and wet paper. Meera stood at the drafting table where the north Calcutta map lay stretched between four brass clamps. The city was a neat lattice of ink: lanes; the tank; the church; the railway cutting; the river, if one looked far enough north. Through it ran Queen’s Road, a double line that should have gone east from Tank Square and ended, as it had for twenty years, at the clock tower.

Instead, it bent.

Not much. A slant no wider than the shadow of a match. But Meera had learned to distrust small things. A line was not a line. A line was a promise. A cartographer did not draw what was there. She drew what the city said it was, and if the city changed its mind, the cartographer changed the ink.

She had marked its position three nights running. The first time, she had called it an error. The second, a slip of the pen. The third was not so easy to name.

She set the brass dividers against the sheet. The scale was one inch to ten chains. The tank was fixed. The church was fixed. The railway cutting was fixed. Only the street had moved. It had pivoted on the tank and swung eleven yards north at its eastern end.

“Harish.”

The boy appeared with a tray. He was twenty, perhaps twenty-one, with a pencil behind one ear and the look of a man who had been standing in the rain. He set down two cups of tea and a tin of biscuits.

“The plate is set true, Miss Roy,” he said. “I checked it before you came.”

“Then the road has moved.”

Harish sipped his tea. “Roads do not move before breakfast.”

“This one has. Eleven yards.”

He leaned over the map. It bore her name in the lower corner: MEERA ROY, ASSISTANT DRAUGHTSMAN, NOVEMBER 1893. Harish traced the bent street with a finger. “Perhaps you have drawn it wrong.”

“May I draw you wrong?” she asked. “If you like, you may take my dividers.”

He measured from the tank to the clock tower. He measured from the clock tower to the street. He measured again. His face did not change, but he did not smile.

“It is wrong,” he said.

“Yes,” said Meera. “It is today.”

Harish looked at her. “What do we do?”

Meera took the chain from the wall. It was a surveyor’s chain, one hundred feet long, its brass tags polished by her father’s thumb. She put it under her arm. “We ask the street.”

The office door closed behind them, and Calcutta opened.

November had made the city dry and red. Gas lamps still guttered in the early light. A bullock cart moved past with empty earthen pots; a rickshaw wallah shouted, “Tank Square! Slow, sir, the road is wet,” though the road was not wet. Meera walked north, the chain swinging at her hip, her white cotton sari dark at the hem. She did not hurry.

Queen’s Road began near the tank, where a white pillar stood under a neem tree. By the old municipal plate, the pillar was the street’s western point. From there, the road should have run east, past the tea stalls and the chandler’s shop, to the clock tower.

The pillar was there. The neem tree was there. The tea stalls were not.

In their place stood new shops, their boards so fresh the paint still smelled of turpentine. A man in a black waistcoat swept dust from a doorway. A woman sold betel leaves from a low stool. The street before Meera ran a little north of the line she had known. It was wider, too, and its drains had been relaid in fresh brick.

She stopped.

“This is not Queen’s Road,” the tea seller said.

He leaned on his cart, a small pot of boiling tea between his feet. He had been watching her. Meera turned to him.

“Excuse me,” she said. “Where is Queen’s Road?”

He pointed with a wooden paddle. “There. Near the new bazaar.”

She followed his finger. The street he meant was visible a hundred yards north, a pale line between the rooftops. It was not the street she had measured three days ago. It was not the street on the municipal plate. It was not even the street on the map she had drawn last week.

“And this?” she asked, touching the plank wall of the nearest shop. “What is this?”

The man shrugged. “This is Nizam Lane. It has always been Nizam Lane.”

“Always?”

“Since I was a boy,” he said. “You are a surveyor’s woman, no? You should know the old names.”

Meera did not answer. She uncoiled the chain. From the white pillar, she counted out a hundred feet along what had once been the beginning of Queen’s Road. The chain ended in a new vegetable market. She counted another fifty. It ended at a drain that had not existed before. She turned toward the clock tower and measured the old line. Where the street should have been, there were the backs of houses, a narrow alley choked with marigolds, and a brick wall painted with an advertisement for a lawyer’s office.

The street had moved. Not only had it moved; it had been replaced by something else, as if the city had slid a new page beneath the old one.

Harish, following half a step behind, said, “Miss Roy, there is a constable.”

A constable in a blue cap came out of the alley. He was young, with a stick under his arm and the careful look of a man who did not wish to be involved.

“Excuse me,” Meera said. “When was this road last walked by the municipal surveyors?”

The constable looked at the street. “No one walks that road after dark,” he said. “The Committee closed it. They say the houses are unsafe.”

“It was open on the last survey.”

“The last survey,” he repeated, as if the words surprised him. “That was a different time.”

Meera wanted to ask how different, but the constable had already stepped back into the alley, leaving the morning to its own errands.

She stood in the red dust and let the facts settle. The street had not merely shifted its angle. It had changed its position. Her hands, usually so steady at the drafting table, were not steady now. The chain was cold against her forearm.

“Eleven yards,” Harish said.

“Yes.”

“If we put the old line back on the map—”

“No.”

He stopped. “No, Miss?”

“No,” she said. “If we put the old line back, we shall be lying. If we put the new line on, we shall be telling the truth. And either way, we shall have to explain why the street is where it is.”

They walked back to the office in silence.

By nine, Meera had laid out three sheets. The first was the official municipal plate, approved in 1888. The second was her working map, updated each week. The third was blank, ruled in light pencil, waiting.

On the first sheet, Queen’s Road ran east. On the second, it bent. On the third, she drew the street as she had found it: a double line, a little north of where it had been, with a red dot at the tank pillar and a red arrow toward the new bazaar.

As she drew, Harish brought old maps from the archive room. They were folded into neat squares, their edges soft as cloth. Meera spread them one by one.

In 1879, Queen’s Road was farther south. In 1883, nearer the tank. In 1886, it had shifted again, and someone had erased the old line with white paint so cleanly that the paper looked raw. In 1890, it was gone entirely; in its place was a blank space, and in the margin, in small official letters, the words: NO ROAD.

“You never noticed this before?” Harish asked.

“I did not look for it,” Meera said. “One does not look for the thing that is missing.”

Mr. Fitch came then. He was the assistant commissioner, a thin British man with a moustache that seemed to have opinions. He wore a white coat grey at the cuffs and carried a leather portfolio under his arm. He stood over the table and looked at the red line.

“What is this?” he asked.

“Queen’s Road,” Meera said. “As it was this morning.”

Mr. Fitch’s mouth tightened. “There is no Queen’s Road.”

“It is on the municipal plate.”

“The municipal plate is wrong.”

Meera met his eyes. “Roads are not usually wrong, sir.”

“They are drawn by people,” he said. “And people make mistakes. The Committee has decided that the line you have marked does not exist. It has never existed. The new map will show only what is sanctioned.”

“Then the street outside my window?” Harish said, quietly. “The one with the new shops?”

Mr. Fitch did not answer. He looked at the red line as if it might bite him. Then he buttoned his coat and left.

Meera waited until his footsteps were gone, then took the 1890 map and held it to the light. The blank space where the street had been was not truly blank. Under the white paint, a faint pencil line showed through: the ghost of a road, erased but not forgotten.

She opened the drawer by her elbow and took out a small notebook. It had belonged to her father. The leather was cracked, the pages brown at the edges. On the last page, in his cramped hand, was a single line.

Do not map it twice. It comes to the mapmaker.

Meera sat very still. The office was quiet except for the tick of the clock and the low hiss of the gas lamp. Outside, the city made its ordinary sounds: a cart wheel on stone, a dog barking, a boy selling flowers. On the blank sheet before her, the red line she had drawn was still wet.

She looked at it.

The line had moved.

Not much. A slant. But the red ink, which should have stayed where she had put it, had shifted eleven yards north at its eastern end. The street on the map was no longer the street she had found in the city. It was something new. It was something coming.

“Miss Roy,” Harish said, from the doorway. “Look.”

She looked.

Outside the louvered window, Hastings Lane was empty. The gas lamps were guttering in the daylight. The dust was still. And the street itself—the line of the drains, the row of tea stalls, the set of the pavement—was moving, slowly, like a river under a bridge. It was not the city moving. It was the street, alone, sliding past the window, carrying its new shops and its fresh brick and its nameless distance with it.

On the map, the red line bent again.

It had come, at last, to the mapmaker.

At half past seven, the Survey Office in Hastings was cool and smelled of lampblack, camphor, and the damp of paper that had spent the night under a wet cloth. Meera stood at the long drafting table where the north Calcutta map lay stretched between four brass clamps. The city was a neat lattice of ink: lanes, lanes, lanes; the tank; the church; the railway cutting; the river, if one looked far enough north. Through all of it ran Queen's Road, a double line that should have gone east from Tank Square and ended, as it had for the last twenty years, at the clock tower.

Instead, it bent.

Not much. A hair's turn. A slant no wider than the shadow of a matchstick. But Meera had learned to distrust small things. In her father's workshop, before the fever took him, he had taught her that a line was not a line. A line was a promise. A cartographer did not draw what was there. She drew what the city said it was, and if the city changed its mind, the cartographer changed the ink.

She set the brass dividers against the corner of the sheet. The scale was one inch to ten chains. The tank was fixed. The church was fixed. The railway cutting was fixed. Only the street had moved. It had pivoted on the tank and swung eleven yards north at its eastern end, as if some invisible hand had taken the map by the collar and nudged it.

"Harish."

The boy appeared in the doorway with a tray. He was twenty, perhaps twenty-one, with a pencil tucked behind one ear and the look of a man who had been standing in the rain. He set down two cups of tea and a tin of biscuits.

"The plate is set true, Miss Roy," he said. "I checked it before you came."

"Then the road has moved."

Harish sipped his tea. "Roads do not move before breakfast."

"This one has. Eleven yards."

He came closer and leaned over the table. The map was the large sheet she had been revising for the Municipal Committee. It bore her name in the lower corner: MEERA ROY, ASSISTANT DRAUGHTSMAN, NOVEMBER 1893. Harish traced the bent street with a finger. "Perhaps you have drawn it wrong."

"May I draw you wrong?" she asked. "If you like, you may take my dividers."

He took them. He measured from the tank to the clock tower. He measured from the clock tower to the street. He measured again. His face did not change, but he did not smile.

"It is wrong," he said.

"Yes," said Meera. "It is today."

Harish looked at her. "What do we do?"

Meera took the chain from the wall. It was a surveyor's chain, one hundred feet long, with brass tags that had been polished by her father's thumb. She put it under her arm. "We ask the street."

The office door closed behind them, and Calcutta opened.

November had made the city dry and red. The dust lay on the lanes like powder from a gun. Gas lamps still guttered in the early light, their blue flames low and tired. A bullock cart moved past the office with a load of empty earthen pots; the bullocks' eyes were large and patient. A rickshaw wallah shouted into the morning, "Tank Square! Tank Square! The pillar was there. The neem tree was there. The tea stalls were not.

In their place stood a row of new shops, their boards so fresh the paint still smelled of turpentine. A man in a black waistcoat was sweeping dust from a doorway. A woman sat on a low stool selling betel leaves. The street before Meera ran a little north of the line she had known. It was wider, too, and its drains had been relaid in fresh brick.

She stopped and looked.

"This is not Queen's Road," the tea seller said.

He was leaning on his cart, a small pot of boiling tea between his feet. He had been watching her. Meera turned to him.

"Excuse me," she said. "Where is Queen's Road?"

He pointed with a wooden paddle. "There. Near the new bazaar."

She followed his finger. The street he meant was visible a hundred yards north, a pale line between the rooftops. It was not the street she had measured three days ago. It was not the street on the municipal plate. It was not even the street on the map she had drawn last week.

"And this?" she asked, touching the plank wall of the nearest shop. "What is this?"

The man shrugged. "This is Nizam Lane. It has always been Nizam Lane."

"Always?"

"Since I was a boy," he said. "You are a surveyor's woman, no? You should know the old names."

Meera did not answer. She uncoiled the chain. From the white pillar, she counted out a hundred feet along what had once been the beginning of Queen's Road. The chain ended in the middle of a new vegetable market. She counted another fifty. It ended at a drain that had not existed before. She turned the chain toward the clock tower and measured the old line. Where the street should have been, there were now the backs of houses, a narrow alley choked with marigolds, and a brick wall painted with an advertisement for a lawyer's office.

The street had moved. Not only had it moved; it had been replaced by something else, as if the city had slid a new page beneath the old one.

The chain was cold against her forearm.

"Yes."

"No."

Mr. Fitch's mouth tightened. "There is no Queen's Road."

Do not map it twice. It comes to the mapmaker.

The line had moved.

It was the street, alone, sliding past the window, carrying its new shops and its fresh brick and its nameless distance with it.

On the map, the red line bent again.

It had come, at last, to the mapmaker.

At half past seven, the Survey Office in Hastings smelled of lampblack, camphor, and wet paper. Meera stood at the drafting table where the north Calcutta map lay stretched between four brass clamps. The city was a neat lattice of ink: lanes; the tank; the church; the railway cutting; the river, if one looked far enough north. Through it ran Queen's Road, a double line that should have gone east from Tank Square and ended, as it had for twenty years, at the clock tower.

Instead, it bent.

Not much. A slant no wider than a match-shadow. But Meera had learned to distrust small things. A line was not a line. A line was a promise. A cartographer did not draw what was there. She drew what the city said it was, and if the city changed its mind, the cartographer changed the ink.

She had marked its position three nights running. The first time, she had called it an error. The second, a slip of the pen. The third was not so easy to name.

She set the brass dividers against the sheet. The scale was one inch to ten chains. The tank was fixed. The church was fixed. The railway cutting was fixed. Only the street had moved. It had pivoted on the tank and swung eleven yards north at its eastern end.

The boy appeared with a tray. He was twenty, perhaps twenty-one, with a pencil behind one ear and the look of a man who had been standing in the rain. He set down two cups of tea and a tin of biscuits.

"Then the road has moved."

Harish sipped his tea. "Roads do not move before breakfast."

A constable in a blue cap came out of the alley. He was young, with a stick under his arm and the careful look of a man who did not wish to be involved.

"Excuse me," Meera said. "When was this road last walked by the municipal surveyors?"

The constable looked at the street. "No one walks that road after dark," he said. "The Committee closed it. They say the houses are unsafe."

"The last survey," he repeated, as if the words surprised him. "That was a different time."

"Yes."

On the first sheet, Queen's Road ran east. On the second, it bent. On the third, she drew the street as she had found it: a double line, a little north of where it had been, with a red dot at the tank pillar and a red arrow toward the new bazaar.

"I did not look for it," Meera said. "One does not look for the thing that is missing."

Mr. Fitch came then. He was the assistant commissioner, a thin British man with a moustache that seemed to have opinions. He wore a white coat grey at the cuffs and carried a leather portfolio under his arm. He stood over the table and looked at the red line.

"What is this?" he asked.

"Queen's Road," Meera said. "As it was this morning."

Mr. Fitch's mouth tightened. "There is no Queen's Road."

"It is on the municipal plate."

"The municipal plate is wrong."

Meera met his eyes. "Roads are not usually wrong, sir."

"They are drawn by people," he said. "And people make mistakes. The Committee has decided that the line you have marked does not exist. It has never existed. The new map will show only what is sanctioned."

Mr. Fitch did not answer. He looked at the red line as if it might bite him. Then he buttoned his coat and left.

She opened the drawer by her elbow and took out a small notebook. It had belonged to her father. The leather was cracked, the pages brown at the edges. On the last page, in his cramped hand, was a single line.

Do not map it twice. It comes to the mapmaker.

Meera sat very still. The office was quiet except for the tick of the clock and the low hiss of the gas lamp. Outside, the city made its ordinary sounds: a cart wheel on stone, a dog barking, a boy selling flowers. On the blank sheet before her, the red line she had drawn was still wet.

She looked at it.

The line had moved.

Not much. A slant. But the red ink, which should have stayed where she had put it, had shifted eleven yards north at its eastern end. The street on the map was no longer the street she had found in the city. It was something new. It was something coming.

"Miss Roy," Harish said, from the doorway. "Look."

She looked.

It was the street, alone, sliding past the window, carrying its new shops and its fresh brick and its nameless distance with it.

On the map, the red line bent again.

It had come, at last, to the mapmaker.
